sprint.name: Data Quality & Foundations
sprint.goal: Turn an untrustworthy customer table into a single source of truth — and quantify the cost of not doing so.

brief.body: The PE firm starts diligence in five weeks. Before we show them a single customer number, I need to know our customer data is clean — last quarter we reported a customer count inflated by duplicates and it was embarrassing. Get the new intern to (a) tell me exactly how bad the duplication is, and (b) hand me one customer table I can actually trust.

tickets.title: Measure the duplication in the customer table
tickets.prompt: Before we clean anything, quantify the problem. Return a single number: how many CustomerIDs appear more than once in the raw customers table.
acceptanceCriteria: Returns one value: the count of CustomerIDs that occur more than once
Counts distinct offending IDs, not total duplicate rows
hints: GROUP BY CustomerID, then keep only groups with COUNT(*) > 1.
Wrap that in an outer COUNT(*) to count how many such IDs there are.

tickets.title: Clean city report — how many phantom cities did the dirty data invent?
tickets.prompt: Raw City is a mess of casing and stray whitespace, so the same city shows up several times. Return a single row with exactly two columns, in this order: (1) the distinct city count BEFORE cleaning, (2) the distinct city count AFTER cleaning (trim + lowercase). This is the 'before vs after' card Sana wants at the top of the report.
acceptanceCriteria: One row, two columns: raw distinct-city count then cleaned distinct-city count
Cleaning handles BOTH whitespace and casing
Column order is raw first, clean second
hints: COUNT(DISTINCT City) gives the raw count.
For the clean count, normalize inside the COUNT: COUNT(DISTINCT TRIM(LOWER(City))).
LOWER alone leaves 'mumbai' and 'mumbai ' as two cities — TRIM is mandatory.

tickets.title: Surface the impossible-revenue orders
tickets.prompt: The orders table has a few rows with impossible revenue that distort every average and margin. Return the OrderID of every order whose Revenue is zero or negative — one column, one row per bad order. Don't drop them silently; we need the list for the audit.
acceptanceCriteria: Returns a single column of OrderIDs
No orders with valid (positive) revenue leak into the list
hints: Select only OrderID — the grader looks at the first column.
